speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: asked the Acting Minister for Transport (a) how does the Ministry evaluate the effectiveness of enforcement on pedestrian-only paths and cycling lanes; (b) whether the Ministry tracks locations with frequent resident feedback on near-misses or safety concerns; (c) whether further measures are planned to enhance pedestrian safety; and (d) if so, what are these measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Path marking and signs are used to demarcate cycling paths, shared paths and pedestrian-only paths (POPs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Clear logos and wordings guide users at areas of potential interaction between pedestrians and cyclists, and to signal transitions between POPs and shared paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: LTA conducts education campaigns and community engagement programmes regularly to promote gracious path sharing and safe behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Enforcement officers conduct regular patrols to ensure adherence to the path segregation of cycling paths and POPs.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I have three supplementary questions pertaining to enforcement.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: One, how is the Ministry working with enforcement officers to ensure consistent and proportionate enforcement of cycling and pedestrian path rules, including when to issue warnings versus fines?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And what does the Minister of State think of licensing cyclists and their vehicles?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: My second question is about recourse when pedestrians are injured by cyclists or personal mobility device riders on footpaths or even overhead bridges, what processes are in place to ensure victims receive prompt support and recourse, and whether the Ministry is reviewing ways to strengthen this safety net?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And the last question is on engagement, whether the Ministry has actively engaged on things like path design, safety hotspots and enforcement, and whether it has plans to expand public education campaigns to emphasise shared responsibility?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The enforcement officers will do their best to ensure that there is a consistent approach to look out for errant behaviour and to mete out the necessary penalties or advisories.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: In the case of POPs, it is relatively new since July 2025.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, the rule is that cyclists or riders are not supposed to go on POPs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But if there are instances, for example, where the cyclist or rider needs to temporarily overtake a slow-moving cyclist on the cycling path and then venture for that instance on the POP, that will not be counted as an offence, because that is understandable as long as he does it in a safe manner, by looking out for other users of the POP.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But when it is obvious that the cyclist or rider is blatantly riding on POPs, without safe regard for other users, over extended distances, then that definitely will be an offence, and the enforcement officers will issue fines.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: In cases where the riders are performing work-related rides, like doing delivery, they are also required to have third-party liability insurance, so that would also cater for any claims for injury.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: On licensing riders or cyclists and vehicles or bicycles, many years ago, Singapore does require registration of bicycles, but it has become a very laborious exercise because bicycles are passed down within families, from people to people, and it becomes an administrative hassle to have to update, not only for the authorities, but for owners of bicycles.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We also take reference from practices and learnings from other countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It is also not easy to license riders because riders span a spectrum of different ages, from the very young to the very old.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, we focus on educational campaigns and rules for riding behaviour.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: That is more sustainable and we will keep on promoting that to ensure a safe riding landscape for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The Member had a last question about getting feedback on the ground.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Yes, we continue to do that, on how better to design our paths, our cycling infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, we will continue our engagements with advisors, grassroots leaders and other community groups.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: In terms of education programmes, we look at schools, community groups and we also do regular engagements with delivery platforms to ensure that the riders are up to date with the rules and exercise due consideration when they ride.
